quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Two Views on Lectures
quests.passage: Professor Alvarez argues that universities should move most lectures online. Recorded lectures, she says, let students pause, rewind and rewatch difficult sections, something a live hall never allows, and the savings on teaching rooms could pay for smaller seminars. Professor Grant disagrees. He accepts that recordings are convenient, but points out that attendance at his live lectures is far higher than views of his recordings, which many students leave unwatched until the week before exams. For him, the value of a live lecture is not only the content but the shared deadline it creates: you must turn up on Tuesday at ten, whether you feel like it or not. Both agree, however, that small discussion groups matter more than either format, and neither would cut them.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Letter of Reference
quests.passage: To whom it may concern, Mr. Daniel Pryce worked as an administrative assistant in our department for two years. He arrived at work on time, kept his desk tidy, and never caused a dispute among colleagues. His filing was accurate, and he was always willing to follow instructions exactly as given. His reports reached us by the stated deadline every time. When asked to cover for a colleague, he did so without complaint. I should add that Mr. Pryce did not seek additional responsibilities and rarely offered suggestions during meetings, though he attended all of them. He left on good terms, and I have no reason to doubt his honesty. I leave it to you to decide whether he suits the position you have in mind.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: The House on Alder Road
quests.passage: Ines had not been inside the house for six years, and she stood in the hallway holding the keys as if they might still be refused. The air smelled of floor polish and old paper. Her brother Marco was already in the kitchen, sorting through drawers with the brisk efficiency he used at work. "There's a buyer," he said, without turning around. "Someone offered above asking." Ines looked at the stairs, at the height marks pencilled on the doorframe, and at the faded rectangle on the wall where a clock had hung. "It's a good offer," she said finally. Marco closed a drawer more gently than he had opened the others. "I know," he said. Neither of them mentioned the clock.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Why Bridges Have Gaps
quests.passage: Drive across almost any large bridge and you will feel a rhythmic thump as the wheels cross the road. Those thumps come from expansion joints, narrow gaps built into the surface at regular intervals. Steel and concrete expand when they are heated and contract when they cool; over a long span, the difference between a freezing night and a hot afternoon can amount to several centimeters. Without gaps to absorb the movement, the road would push against itself and buckle, much like a rug pushed from both ends. The gaps are covered with interlocking metal teeth or flexible seals so that traffic can cross smoothly. Engineers accept the small noise as the price of a bridge that lasts.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: The Middle Option
quests.passage: Menus are rarely written by accident. Consider a café offering a small coffee at $3 and a large at $5. Many customers choose the small, as they prefer to save money. Now add a medium at $4.80. Almost nobody buys the medium; its purpose is to make the large look like a bargain, since for just twenty cents more you get a bigger cup. Marketers call the unwanted medium a decoy, and experiments suggest it can raise large-cup sales noticeably. Customers believe they are making a rational comparison, but the comparison was designed for them. None of this proves the café is dishonest; the large coffee is not a bad deal. It simply shows that the order in which we are shown choices shapes the choices we make.

quests.passageTopic: Opinion: The Quiet Cost of Easy Grades
quests.passage: Over twenty years, the share of top grades at our local university has risen from 18 percent to 46 percent. Defenders say students are simply working harder or being taught better. Perhaps. But if that were true, we would expect employers to report stronger graduates, and instead many say they now rely on their own tests because grades no longer tell them who is capable. When almost half the class receives the top mark, the mark stops distinguishing anyone. The harm falls hardest on the best students, who lose the recognition their work deserves, and on those who struggle, who are denied honest feedback until too late. Universities should not blame students for responding to incentives; they should reform the incentives.

quests.passageTopic: Museum Audio Guide: The Market at Dusk
quests.passage: Stand a few steps back from this painting and let your eye settle. At first you may see a cheerful scene: stalls, baskets of fruit, a vendor laughing. Now look at the edges. At the lower left, a child holds out an empty hand; at the right, a woman counts coins and frowns at the total. The artist painted this in 1893, a year of widespread unemployment, and critics at the time complained that the painting was too gloomy for a market scene. Others argued that the cheerfulness at the center was itself the point: the painter shows the surface of commerce, and the cost of it at the margins. As you look again, ask yourself where the artist wants your attention to rest.
